summary: Teaches rounding two-decimal-place numbers to the nearest whole and to one decimal place, treating rounding as choosing between two neighbouring values at a chosen precision, decided by the single digit immediately to the right of the target place. Two central traps: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is linked to estimation (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7); for this particular pair the rounding errors cancel, so the estimate equals the true sum. A zoomable number line is the lead activity because the same number can be rounded to different precisions and the carry can be watched; a set of checkable questions, a static annotated line, and diagnostic prompts are preserved as complementary tools.
misconceptions: Double rounding: 3.47 → 3.5 → 4 to the nearest whole
Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (or a chain of digits) when rounding to a whole
Drops the boundary carry: 12.95 → 12.10 or 12.9 instead of 13.0
Omits the trailing zero / place: writes 13 when 1dp is asked, or truncates

activities.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
steps: Plot 3.47 on a number line showing whole numbers 3 and 4; mark the 3.5 midpoint and judge that 3.47 sits just below it, so it is nearer 3.

Deliberately try the tempting wrong path: round 3.47 to 3.5 first, then watch 3.5 round up to 4 — the WRONG whole. Compare side by side with going straight from 3.47 (tenths digit 4, below half) which gives 3.
Zoom the line to tenths and round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).

Switch to a 12.9–13.0 view and round 12.95 to one decimal place; notice it sits exactly halfway, so by the usual rule (a deciding 5 rounds up) it snaps to 13.0, and watch the whole-number digit tick from 12 to 13 as the carry ripples in.

Use an estimation view to round 4.83 and 2.17 each to the nearest whole and add (5 + 2 = 7); then compare with the true sum (7.00) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal — here rounding 4.83 up and 2.17 down cancel, so the estimate equals the true total.
activities.insight: Round in ONE step from the original number; to the nearest whole only the tenths digit decides, so 3.47 → 3. The boundary carry (12.95 → 13.0) is a real event where a rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole, not a rule failure.

activities.title: Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart
steps: Place a number such as 3.47 in a place-value chart and name the place you are rounding to.
Point to the ONE digit immediately to the right of that place as the sole decider before rounding — for rounding to a whole, the tenths digit (4); for rounding to 1dp, the hundredths digit.
Explain why the 7 (hundredths) does NOT decide the nearest whole of 3.47.
activities.insight: The deciding digit is exactly the one place to the right of the target place (the tenths when rounding to a whole, the hundredths when rounding to 1dp) — never a chain of digits.

activities.title: Checkable rounding and estimation questions
steps: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (answer 3).

Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole (5 + 2 = 7) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the true total (7.00) — for this pair the rounding errors cancel, so it is exactly equal.
activities.insight: A learner can round correctly to a stated precision in one step and use rounding to estimate and sense-check a sum.

activities.title: Diagnostic sequence and probing questions
steps: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, then round 3.47 to one decimal place; say which single digit tells you each answer and why not the 7.
Round 12.95 to one decimal place and explain what happens to the whole-number part and why.
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole; then say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the real total.
If you said 3.5 and then 4 for the nearest whole, redo it going straight from 3.47 — which whole is it actually nearer?
activities.insight: Explaining the deciding digit and the carry, in one step from the original, distinguishes secure rounding from double rounding, dropped/mishandled carry, and truncation.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, and then round 3.47 to one decimal place. Next, round 12.95 to one decimal place. Finally, estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding.' Watch each step — especially whether they go via 3.5 for the whole, and what happens to 12.95.
checkAnswer: 3.47 → 3 (nearest whole; tenths digit is 4) and 3.5 (to 1dp); 12.95 → 13.0 (to 1dp, the carry ripples into the whole); 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7.
